lesson.grammar_point: formal linking devices and be to, be supposed to and have to in executive writing

listenings.text: I ask every writer on my team to picture one reader: an investor in another time zone, opening our release at six in the morning, on a phone, in her second language. She will read the first sentence. She may read the second. After that, we have to earn every line. That is why I cut adjectives before anything else. Distinguished, historic and landmark tell her nothing she can use. What she needs are the relationships between facts, and English gives us small words to show them before the fact arrives. Whereas tells her a contrast is coming. Albeit tells her we are about to limit what we just said. In light of tells her the cause. Get those right, and a reader in her second language can follow a complex argument without effort.

Let me make your life easier by explaining how journalists like me actually work. If you tell me something on the record, I can print it and put your name on it. If you tell me something on background, I can use the information, but I will describe you only as a person familiar with the matter. If you want nothing printed at all, you have to say so before you tell me, not after. And if your release is under embargo until six, I will respect that, but only if the embargo is on the email itself. A final piece of advice. When something goes wrong, send a short holding statement early. Silence is what makes a small story big.

reading.rtitle: Four Drafts of the Same Release
paras: The first draft of almost every press statement begins with the organization: who hosted the event, where it took place, and how many distinguished participants attended. It is accurate, and it is useless. An investor in Toronto opening the email at six in the morning wants to know one thing: what changed today. That answer belongs in the lede, the first sentence, and it should be the only fact the reader needs if they stop there.

The second draft usually fixes the lede but loses the key message. Every paragraph adds something true, whereas none of them points in the same direction. By contrast, a good release chooses one idea and makes each sentence support it. If the key message is that the ministry and the funds have found common ground, a paragraph about the venue does not help, albeit pleasing to the sponsor.

The third draft is where the lawyers arrive, and for good reason. Anything that could change an investor’s decision is material information, and listed companies in the room have disclosure obligations. Consequently, the words that describe commitments matter more than the adjectives. A ministry that is to publish rules by March has a plan. A report that was supposed to come out in June is a promise that failed. Operators that have to comply within ninety days face an obligation. Mixing the three is the fastest way to lose credibility.

The fourth draft is the one that goes out. It is shorter than the first, the quote from the spokesperson is clearly on the record, and anything shared on background has been removed. It carries an embargo until the markets close, and the boilerplate sits quietly at the bottom. Notwithstanding all this work, the best test is simple: read the first sentence aloud to somebody who was not in the room. If they can repeat it, the release is ready.
reading.source: Written for this lesson, from standard practice in corporate and institutional communications.

items.situation: Your comms team wrote a first sentence about the venue and the number of participants. Tell them what the lede should say instead.
tips: The lede has to say what changed today: that the funds and the ministry agreed to study international arbitration.
has to for an obligation; what changed today is the test.

items.situation: Say that investment grew, but from a very low starting point, in one written-style sentence.
tips: Investment grew sharply, albeit from a very low base.
albeit + a short phrase, never a full sentence.

items.situation: A journalist asks whether the concession review is late. Answer precisely.
tips: It was supposed to be published in June, and it is now expected in the first quarter.
was supposed to reports a plan that did not happen.

items.situation: Contrast the fund’s position and the ministry’s position in one sentence.
tips: The funds want arbitration abroad, whereas the ministry prefers local courts.
whereas joins two clauses that contrast.

items.situation: A journalist wants to quote the arbitration figures a fund manager mentioned privately. Say no, politely.
tips: Those figures were shared on background, so we cannot put them on the record.
on background = use it, do not name the source.

items.situation: Announce the ministry’s next step as an official plan.
tips: In light of today’s discussion, the ministry is to present a draft model by March.
be to + verb sounds official and planned.
